title: Final Year Project
source_note: This is a practical/process course, not a taught-syllabus subject: it is the Computer Science final year software project. Questions cover the standard Nigerian university software-project structure (problem definition, review of existing systems, system analysis and design, implementation and testing, conclusion) rather than fabricated CS trivia.

questions.question: What are the key components typically contained in Chapter One (Introduction) of a Computer Science final year project?
questions.mark_scheme: Chapter One typically includes the background of the study, statement of the problem the software/system addresses, aim and objectives, significance of the study, scope and limitations of the system, and definition of key terms.

questions.question: How does the literature review (Chapter Two) of a software project typically differ from a purely theory-based literature review?
questions.mark_scheme: Besides reviewing relevant theoretical/technical concepts, a software project's Chapter Two typically includes a review of existing/related systems or tools that address similar problems, critically comparing their features and shortcomings, and using this comparison to justify the gap or improvement the new system provides.

questions.question: What is typically covered in the System Analysis and Design chapter of a final year project?
questions.mark_scheme: This chapter covers analysis of the existing system/problem, requirements gathering (functional and non-functional requirements), the chosen development methodology (e.g. Waterfall, Agile/Iterative, Object-Oriented Analysis and Design), and design artefacts such as use case diagrams, entity-relationship diagrams, system architecture and database design.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe two common software development methodologies a final year project might adopt.
questions.mark_scheme: Examples include the Waterfall model (sequential phases: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, each completed before the next begins) and Agile/Iterative development (short cycles of design-implement-test that allow the system to evolve incrementally based on feedback). Other acceptable answers include the spiral model or object-oriented analysis and design (OOADM).

questions.question: What is the difference between the design phase and the implementation phase of a software project?
questions.mark_scheme: Design specifies how the system will be structured and how it will work (architecture, data models, interface layout, algorithms) before any code is written. Implementation is the actual coding/construction of the system based on that design, using the chosen programming language(s) and tools.

questions.question: What types of testing should be carried out on a final year software system, and why is testing important?
questions.mark_scheme: Testing typically includes unit testing (individual components/functions), integration testing (components working together) and system testing (the whole system against requirements), sometimes followed by user acceptance testing. Testing is important to verify the system works correctly, meets its stated requirements, and to catch bugs before deployment/demonstration.

questions.question: What should the Implementation and Results chapter of a final year project present?
questions.mark_scheme: It should describe the tools/languages/frameworks used to build the system, present evidence of the working system (e.g. screenshots or sample outputs), describe how it was tested, and discuss the results against the objectives set out in Chapter One.

questions.question: What should the concluding chapter of a Computer Science final year project contain?
questions.mark_scheme: It should summarise what was built and achieved, state conclusions about whether the objectives were met, discuss the system's limitations, and recommend areas for future improvement or extension of the system.

questions.question: Why must source code and other supporting materials typically be included as an appendix or supplementary submission for a final year project?
questions.mark_scheme: Including the source code (and materials like a user manual or database schema) lets examiners verify that the system was actually built as described, assess code quality, and reproduce or test its functionality if needed.

questions.question: What is a project proposal defense, and what purpose does it serve for a software project before full development begins?
questions.mark_scheme: It is a presentation of the planned project (problem, objectives, proposed system design/methodology) to a departmental panel, which assesses whether the proposed system is feasible, sufficiently scoped and technically sound before implementation starts. Feedback is used to refine the plan.

questions.question: Explain plagiarism in the context of a software project, including both the written report and the code.
questions.mark_scheme: Plagiarism includes copying another person's written text without attribution, and also submitting someone else's source code (or an unmodified open-source project) as one's own original work. Universities typically require an originality/similarity check on the written report, and supervisors also assess whether the code demonstrates the student's own understanding.

questions.question: What is the role of the project supervisor throughout a Computer Science final year project?
questions.mark_scheme: The supervisor guides the choice of a feasible project topic and technology stack, reviews the system design and implementation progress, helps troubleshoot technical issues, and certifies that the completed system and report are ready for defense/submission.

questions.question: Why is it important for a final year project report to clearly state the scope and limitations of the system built?
questions.mark_scheme: Clearly stating scope defines exactly what features/functions the system covers, while limitations honestly note constraints (e.g. platform, data, performance, features not implemented) so examiners assess the work fairly against what was actually promised and delivered.
